walkthroughs.body_html:
Human Nutrition — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Human Nutrition brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Human Nutrition.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
options: Human skin cell
Yeast
Bacterium
Onion cell
protein synthesis
photosynthesis
aerobic respiration
cell division
A series of chemical reactions in cells that break down glucose to release energy as ATP.
Respiration is the process by which plants make their own food using sunlight.
Respiration means breathing — inhaling oxygen and exhaling carbon dioxide.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
Its tertiary structure (3D shape) changes, particularly the active site, so it can no longer bind substrate effectively.
Ribosomes synthesise amino acids from scratch using the mRNA as a template.

mcqs.q: What reads the mRNA codons during translation?
options: Ribosomes synthesise amino acids from scratch using the mRNA as a template.
DNA directly reads the codons on mRNA and adds amino acids.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
tRNA molecules carrying specific amino acids — their anticodons pair with mRNA codons at the ribosome.

mcqs.q: A bacterium is 2 µm long. How many fit end-to-end across a 1 mm gap?
options: 250 bacteria
500 bacteria
750 bacteria
400 bacteria

mcqs.q: A student adds amylase to starch solution and tests with iodine every minute. The blue-black colour gradually disappears. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Amylase has broken the starch down into sugars.
Starch has turned into protein.
The iodine has been used up by the enzyme.
Amylase builds starch from glucose.

mcqs.q: Bile is added to a fat-and-water mixture and the fat breaks into tiny droplets. What is bile doing and why does it help digestion?
options: Emulsifying fat to increase surface area for lipase.
Chemically digesting fat into glucose.
Neutralising the fat so it cannot be digested.
Acting as an enzyme that breaks peptide bonds.

mcqs.q: The small intestine is lined with villi. How do villi improve absorption of digested food?
options: They greatly increase the surface area for absorption.
They produce enzymes that build large molecules.
They slow food down so it cannot be absorbed.
They carry out respiration for the gut.

mcqs.q: A meal is low in iron over many weeks. Which deficiency is most likely to result?
options: Anaemia (too few healthy red blood cells)
Scurvy
Rickets
Goitre

sequence.def: Teeth chew; amylase begins starch digestion
Peristalsis pushes the bolus to the stomach
